transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News, I'm Dale Willman.
In Brazil's presidential race,
the right-wing opposition candidate is in the lead
after almost all votes have been counted
in Sunday's first round of voting.
It's an election with stakes that reach far beyond
the South American country's borders.
Catherine Osborne has more from Rio de Janeiro.
In downtown Rio, supporters of left-wing president
Luis Ignacio Lula da Silva packed into this plaza,
watching the results with anxiety.
Right-wing senator Flavio Bolsonaro
outperformed polls and outperformed Lula
to win the first-round presidential vote.
He's promised to continue the legacy of his father,
former president Jair Bolsonaro.
In this election, right-wing politicians
also grew in numbers in Brazil's congress.
The presidential runoff is set for October 25th.
It's a contest President Trump is watching closely
as he seeks greater U.S. influence in the region.
For NPR News, I'm Catherine Osborne in Rio de Janeiro.
President Trump has named a new czar
who will oversee AI policy.
He'll also help lead a new White House team
that will be focused on AI technology.
NPR's Shondalise Duster has more on our story.
President Trump says Director of National Intelligence
Jay Clayton is the new White House AI czar
and will help lead his superintelligence force.
After Trump's meeting with AI leaders last week,
Clayton pushed back on calls
to pause developing the technology
during an interview with CNBC.
To somehow say we should back away from this
and let the rest of the world develop these models
and implement these models,
I don't think anybody in that room,
and I don't think any American,
should think that that's a good strategy.
It's unclear what Clayton's appointment as AI czar
means for the AI industry
as current artificial intelligence regulation
by the U.S. government is limited.
Shondalise Duster, NPR News.
Americans are continuing to feel a financial squeeze
from record high energy costs.
The AAA says the national average of a gallon of diesel
remains at $6.34.
Before the U.S. attacked Iran,
a gallon cost $3.76.
Speaking on CBS Sunday, Energy Secretary Chris Wright
said that President Trump knew what would happen
to fuel costs before he launched the war.
He was well aware of the risk to energy flows
that were coming out of the Persian Gulf region.
He said, "I simply cannot,
the world cannot sustain a nuclear-armed Iran,
and I'm not going to do it."
Trump attacked Iran in 2025,
saying then he had destroyed its nuclear capabilities.
Police say they still have no motive
for a shooting early Sunday morning
at a homecoming party in Vienna, Georgia.
At least two people were killed
and almost three dozen others injured.
The victims were taken to several area hospitals.
The party was spread across four blocks of the city,
and police were on patrol when the shooting began.
So far, there have been no arrests.
You're listening to NPR News.
Days before the first anniversary of the Gaza ceasefire,
new assessments by U.N. agencies
warned that basic humanitarian needs in Gaza
are far from being resolved.
NPR's Anas Baba reports from Gaza.
The World Health Organization said Friday
the approval process for medical supplies
can last two and a half months for Israeli clearance.
And if the supplies are rejected,
the process starts over.
Israeli authorities classify some restricted equipment
as dual use with potential military applications,
but the WHO disputes that characterization,
noting many are standard medical supplies used globally.
Meanwhile, the World Food Program
warns a funding shortfall is cutting the number of people
receiving monthly food assistance to 600,000,
down from 1.1 million.
That leaves two-thirds of Gaza's population
in crisis-level hunger.
And with winter approaching,
the U.N. notes about 1.7 million people remain displaced,
many without advocate shelter, water, or sanitation.
Anas Baba, NPR News, Gaza.
A search has been suspended off the Massachusetts coast
for six people on an air ambulance
that disappeared during a flight from Bermuda to Boston.
The decision was made on Sunday
after authorities had searched more than 4,400 miles.
Police in Japan say they've arrested a U.S. Marine
on suspicion of killing a 39-year-old local woman.
The woman's body was found in her hotel room
and she appeared to have been strangled to death.
Police say that security footage from the hotel
shows the 29-year-old Marine
entering the hotel with the victim and later leaving alone.
I'm Dale Willman, NPR News.

topics.text: Right-wing senator Flavio Bolsonaro wins Brazil's first-round presidential vote, outperforming left-wing incumbent Lula
President Trump names Jay Clayton as White House AI czar to oversee artificial intelligence policy
National average diesel price remains at $6.34 per gallon after Trump's attack on Iran
At least two killed, nearly three dozen injured in shooting at homecoming party in Vienna, Georgia
U.N. agencies report basic humanitarian needs in Gaza remain unresolved ahead of ceasefire anniversary
Search suspended off Massachusetts coast for six people on air ambulance missing from Bermuda to Boston
U.S. Marine arrested in Japan on suspicion of killing 39-year-old local woman in her hotel room
